summary: Points out that the FTP mail protocol of the day had no way to state the author, title and date of a message, so each system sent them in its own format and programs struggled to process mail. The authors propose standardizing header information.

plainLanguage.summary: Early network mail had no agreed place to write who sent a message, when, and what it was about, so computers could not read those details. This note proposes one shared layout for them as a stopgap.

questions: what headers did early arpanet mail use
subtitle: An interim proposal to give network mail one standard From, Date and Subject header.

tldr.problem: The FTP mail protocol had no way to state the author, title and date of a message, so every system sent that information in its own format and programs could not process mail properly.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose a short header block of FROM, DATE and SUBJECT lines, plus optional keyword lines, followed by a blank line and the message text.
tldr.outcome: It is offered as a quick interim fix, while the long-term answer is expected to be new commands in the mail protocol itself, and the unit metadata shows RFC 680 later updated it.

facts.label: Main header items
facts.value: FROM, DATE, SUBJECT (each at most once)

facts.label: Other items
facts.value: Any number of keyword items, after the main ones

facts.label: Time format
facts.value: Four decimal digits, no internal punctuation

today: RFC 561 has no formal status recorded in the unit metadata, which also lists RFC 680 as an update to it. It was written as an interim proposal while the mail protocol itself was expected to change.

sections.title: The Problem with Mail Headers
sections.content:
The FTP mail protocol makes no provision for explicitly specifying header information such as author, title and date. Many systems send that information, but each in a different format. The authors call the result fairly serious: it is next to impossible for a system or user program to intelligently process incoming mail.

The long-term solution is probably to add commands for such information to the mail protocol command space, as suggested in RFC 524. This RFC proposes a quicker interim answer instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Because everyone wrote the sender and date differently, programs could not understand them. One shared layout fixes that.

sections.title: The Proposed Header Syntax
sections.content:
The proposal covers the text of network mail sent either over the FTP Telnet connection with the MAIL command or over a separate data connection with the MLFL command. The mail text is a header, a blank line, then the message.

The header holds a FROM: item, a DATE: item and a SUBJECT: item, each written as a keyword, a colon, a space and a value. Other keyword: items may follow any number of times, which the RFC calls a misc item. The example header begins with From: White at SRI-ARC, a date of 24 JUL 1973 1527-PDT, a subject and a NIC number.
sections.plainLanguage: At the top of every message come three lines: who it is from, the date and time, and what it is about. Then a blank line, then the message.

sections.title: Rules and Recommendations
sections.content:
The author, date and subject items may each appear at most once, in any order, but all of them must come before any misc item. The case of keywords is insignificant, so From, from and FROM all mean the same thing.

The format of the user name is not legislated beyond excluding spaces, the time carries no internal punctuation, and no provision is made for multiple authors. The authors recommend that mail-sending subsystems which prefix header information to a message be modified accordingly, and that other hosts recommend these conventions to their users.
sections.plainLanguage: The three main lines can come in any order and capital letters do not matter. Each message has a single author.

data.title: Example mail text
data.code:
From: White at SRI-ARC
Date: 24 JUL 1973 1527-PDT
Subject: Multi-Site Journal Meeting Announcement
NIC: 17996

At 10 AM Wednesday 25-JULY there will be a meeting
to discuss a Multi-Site Journal in the context of
the Utility.  Y'all be here.

references.text: White, J., "A Proposed Mail Protocol", RFC 524, June 1973.
